title: Maui Mayor Candidate Forum – Haʻikū Community Association (July 29th, 2026)

recap.headline: Haʻikū Community Association holds forum for Maui County mayor candidates
recap.in_60_seconds: The Haʻikū Community Association held a forum for candidates for Mayor of Maui County at its community center in Haʻikū, ahead of the August 8 primary. Nine candidates took part, seated at two tables, with 90-second opening statements, one-minute answers kept by a timekeeper, and turns going back and forth between the tables. The moderators said the questions came from across the community. They covered water access for Haʻikū families, speed tables on Haʻikū roads, control of East Maui ditch water, funding for the invasive species program MISC, a Haʻikū fire station, and help for owners converting cesspools to septic systems.

answers.summary: Said he is a former NASA engineer who came to Maui after seeing the reefs in 1985 and is running over wastewater sanitation after asking for five years for investment in it. Said he has 12 legislative ideas posted at livingmaui.org/legislation, including a bump-off act that would compensate residents like a class action settlement.

Said his family includes pig and taro farmers, including from Kahakuloa, and that his military veteran parents raised him in Kahului. Said Haʻikū shares countywide challenges his administration has been addressing: keeping families home on Maui, traffic safety, public safety and caring for natural resources, and that he intends to finish what he started.

Described himself as a retired U.S. Navy SEAL, Vietnam veteran, former Department of Education worker, federal law enforcement instructor, and a Haʻikū banana and avocado farmer for 30 years. Said he has worked toward a permanent county farmers market, found a parking area for homeless people that could open in one month, and will eliminate corruption and fraud.

Said that at 41 he would treat the job as all day and all night, auditing spending and reallocating money to community-focused uses, drawing on handling millions of dollars for companies. Urged more community gatherings and said turnout among voters aged about 17 to 30 is 5 to 7%, calling for more young people to vote.

Said she is a 36-year Maui resident living in Lahaina with a business degree, and turned a company from bankruptcy to a sale of almost $100 million in two and a half years. Said the county's $1.6 billion budget grew 46.7% in three years, called herself the cost cutter, and cited plans for affordable homes and rolling back the gas tax and registration fees.

Said she is 25, from a five-generation farming family, and is running because the county has been reactive instead of proactive, citing dumping. Said she has researched solutions used elsewhere and that their cost should be taxed from those who can afford it, not regular residents, so fewer people are forced from their homes.

Said they were born and raised on Maui, where their father, a physician, did house calls in Haʻikū, and that they are 10 years in the council, a 247 job. Said their administration will live by transparency and communication, and the Haʻikū fire station won't have a final decision until August the 10th, with community input.

Said he was born in Silverton, Oregon, raised around Maui including Kīhei, Haʻikū, Makawao and Pukalani, and graduated from Maui High School in 2001. Said he served eight years in the Marine Corps, applied to the police and fire departments, and wants accountability, safety and for everyone in Maui County to thrive.

Said he is running because of a fire that was not a wildfire, and asked where the massive recovery grant went. Criticized the mayor and the council for three years with no business rebuilding in Lahina, and accused Oʻahu legislators of blocking reconstruction for mainland developer donors who want the land.

questions.question: As mayor, what specific actions will you take to provide water for the hundreds of Haʻikū families who have no access to a public water supply and are not on the Upcountry water list?

answers.summary: Supports bringing Maui's water systems under county control so assets can be monitored, maintained and allocated, letting Upcountry residents get meters. Said the county must check a system's infrastructure and repair costs before buying it, and that 30 years is too long to wait for a water meter.

Said the county should audit water systems before buying them, since repairs would cost money. Proposed finding where the water is going and redirecting it from the mountain to the sea so residents don't have to conserve water every three months.

Said he applied for a second water meter in 2002, got it in 2025, and was billed for 20,000 gallons on an unconnected meter, which the department called a mistake. Said the county needs objectives and a plan with a timeline for its water goals, and that he has heard from department staff that people may be drinking sewage water.

Said water is a public trust that the community should control, and that this is under way. Said he testified before the Board of Land and Natural Resources for a set-aside of the East Maui Irrigation system and at the Office of Hawaiian Affairs, saying private businesses can sell or abandon water systems.

Proposed securing resources, doing a system level analysis and connecting all meters through a ticket program. Cited the Nani Act, which gives rights to ecosystems, to restore the stream flow. Said the conversation about moving water over there should wait until after sanitation, and noted his NASA systems engineer job.

Said Maui has abundant groundwater filtered by sand and minerals, and that drilling would provide enough water for everyone. Said the questions were being controlled and did not include the issues that matter most.

Said water is a public trust and Haʻikū's source can supply seven million gallons a day while about 3.5 million is used, so she would increase a plant's capacity to serve the 455 people on the meter list. Said a consent decree stops water being taken from Haʻikū and she would ask corporation counsel to review it.

Proposed restoring streams and watersheds, saying natural stream processes produce water, and said water is a human right the county should control. Proposed reintroducing rain barrel incentives that she said were cut for lack of funding.

Proposed building more water catchments, using some land to serve a growing population. Said water should go to residents first rather than to empty luxury condos, and that Haʻikū could be the pioneer.

questions.question: If you are mayor, what would you do about the speed table situation?

answers.summary: Said he would take all the speed tables out. Used the rest of his time to say Hawaiʻi is under an illegal occupation of the Hawaiian Kingdom that must be addressed, and that there were no questions on the fire or fraud.

Credited Haʻikū residents and an earlier presenter for raising the issue and said she will attend the August 26 meeting. Said as mayor she would consult the community and get feedback before installing things like speed bumps, which she said are for safety.

Proposed removing speed bumps not built to code and holding the contractor and others accountable. Said her Nextdoor poll found the number of bumps was the main problem, and called for researching other safety solutions that protect cars and let emergency vehicles through.

Said he would like to remove the speed bumps because they slow emergency responders. Proposed instead a $10,000 fine for driving 5 mph over the limit and $20,000 for 10 mph over, with the money going to infrastructure repair.

Thanked residents, including one who drove the roads with him, and said the county has agreed to remove some speed bumps. Said the decisions were made in 2020 and 2021 after council hearings with community input, and that the August 26 meeting will cover how it happened and what will be done.

Said a resident who is not a county employee researched the issue and the county should follow his course with a timeline. Said a new mayor should order a full investigative audit going back to 2023 and before, check that staff and contractors are qualified, and cited $1.3 million for a safe parking pilot.

Said the county spent money on speed bumps that lifted trucks fly over and will now pay "30 to $45,000" to take out each one. Said it reflects people not being held accountable for their jobs and called for proactive decisions that generate money for the county.

Said she counted 38 speed bumps from Hayeku to Pukalani, put down because of bad engineering or a lucrative contract. Proposed removing them, reviewing where they're necessary, such as pedestrian areas, schools and really crazy curves, and adding traffic cameras whose fines help with road repair.

Cited his bump-off act to remove speed bumps and compensate residents like a class action, and a digital direct democracy act letting residents sign by phone to put ordinances on the ballot to decide where bumps go. Also cited an app to connect health care services.

questions.question: As mayor, would you ask the governor to issue an executive order letting the county take water from the East Maui ditch systems and transfer it to the East Maui Water Authority for Upcountry and Central Valley use, and what would you do to secure control of this resource?

answers.summary: Said she would ask the governor to grant the water rights and entrust the East Maui Water Authority to manage them because it is not for-profit. Opposes giving water rights to a company and said water should be shared equally and kept in public hands.

Said a governor's emergency proclamation would apply only to state land and is limited but can help. Supports finding more water sources and the East Maui Water Authority investigating its powers regarding EMI.

Proposed letting private owners drill their own wells so streams keep flowing, and said less water should be taken from the east side. Said community control is better than a private corporation, but the government wastes money, so he would be cautious with both.

Said he doesn't have all the answers and is still studying the issue, and would ask Maui High School graduates he knows to help. Said outside corporations don't deserve the water and it should stay in Maui, Maui County, Mokai and Lai.

Said any diverted water must be sanitized and cleaned so people aren't made sick elsewhere on the island. Endorsed Travis's water plans, and called for one giant 20-year plan instead of doing things a few years at a time.

Said water is a public trust but appurtenant water rights in some deeds must be honored. Called for 5- to 20-year planning to acquire water systems, map unmapped aquifers and build delivery, storage and transmission systems, which she said will be expensive.

Said his Y act zeros out property taxes on properly managed wheds for Kūlana lands and increases property taxes on ultra high value real estate holdings, and can pay for the wells. Said this place is under attack and should be treated with military precision, with someone apolitical at the top.

Supports any means for the state to give Maui control of its water, describing an executive order, an emergency proclamation and a set-aside as different tools. Prefers a set-aside letting the county stand in for the state in granting water licenses, so local people decide allocations for farmers and other agricultural uses.

Said any plans affecting the community, whether state or county, need to go before the people first so they can review and understand them, and offered to take a county water tank on his two-acre property. Proposed having people from Maui Correctional Facility do water treatment at no cost, and asked why some of about 600 county openings aren't being used.

questions.question: If elected mayor, do you have a plan to increase and sustain funding for MISC, the invasive species program?

answers.summary: Said he would have experts reassess the work, map all affected locations and review the budget. Proposed focusing on where coquí frogs and other invasive species are spreading most to eliminate large infested areas while still covering all areas.

Said county spending should be reviewed back to inception to cut what is not working and move money to programs like this, citing coconut rhinoceros beetle damage. Said from his own invasive species removal work that crews return every year without cutting deep enough.

Said on day one she would order a forensic audit of the $1.6 billion county budget and the $1.6 billion FEMA gave the county, citing a $200 million carryover fund doing nothing. Said MISK could easily be funded because money will be found when the audit is done. Said a peer review supposed to happen every three years hasn't happened in eight years.

Proposed his Maui Living ʻĀina Stabilization Trust act, creating a coin so donors such as data center investors could give large sums, and raising wages above $17 an hour. Said he lived next to the greenhouse where coquí frogs were introduced and called for a target date and expanded funding.

Said the county funds MISK $2.8 million every year to battle fire ants, ki frogs, the miconia and recently the coconut rhinoceros beetle, and that funding has continued during his term. Said MISK decides employee pay, grant recipients must file a report on how funds were spent, and he continues to favor supporting and funding MISK.

Said the council doubled MISK funding to $2.8 million, from closer to a million, after being told doubling it would get rid of Kyifrogs. Said MISK gets another two million from the state, it takes a community, and her office recently met with MISK. Supports MISK.

Called MISK pivotal to the island and said funding should increase, along with programs to train people for positions that have been empty for so long throughout the county. Said this would help locals get jobs so more people are in the field to address invasive species.

Said he would take whatever funds we have from MISK, bet it on Max Holloway to beat McGregor again, double the income, and pay emergency first responders a living wage starting at $100,000. Said educators deserve a living wage as well, and that he could probably ask for help with budgeting.

Said MSK is cool, but he doesn't like pesticides or insecticides and was a little suspicious about what they were doing. Said there will be no invasive species when they resolve the illegal occupation and are one with the Aina, tuning into Hawaiian culture.

questions.question: Months and years go by and Haʻikū still has no fire station; if elected mayor, do you have a plan to speed it up?

answers.summary: Said the station should have been done yesterday given the $1.6 billion recovery grant. Described himself as a FEMA-trained incident commander and Maui Emergency Management Agency trainer who applied for the job of the official who did not sound sirens, and said officials are stealing the money.

Said the council deferred a decision to August 10; the county acquired the land 17 years ago, dropped a helipad after concerns, and assessed four sites in 2021. Said it will cost about $15 million and would lower homeowner insurance, that she plans to vote on it, and invited residents to the housing and land use committee.
Said federal funding for the station was cut and proposed the county seek reimbursement so the cost does not fall only on local tax dollars.
Said he is not familiar with the situation and would seek collaboration with fellow candidates and his team to put safety first and use the land to build a fire station.

Said the county council's infrastructure committee has failed miserably, citing the unbuilt Olawalo fire station; she lives in Lahina. Said the county has not collaborated with land owners, and that the permitting process and land acquisition need to move forward instead of committees.

Said that if a gentleman told him "That's my Kiana land," he would say "Duly noted. Never mind." Said that with a change in the framework of currency or a donor offering $15 billion, the constraint would no longer be there, then spoke about Tulsi and Iran.

Said residents deserve the 15th fire station in the county of Maui, and that about $15 million in federal funding was cut when the new administration came in. Said the county put those funds in its budget so funding will not be the reason it's not built, and that he is not familiar with the land issue.
Said that with the issue now raised publicly, the county has created a liability and should build the station right away.

Said the issue is lives, not insurance savings, noting an extra 10 minutes for a fire truck can cost a house or a life. Called for acting without years of delay and proposed a phone app so residents can give input and vote on projects.

questions.question: What can you do as mayor to help people who cannot afford to bring their septic systems up to what the law requires for the community's health and safety?

answers.summary: Said he would build a team to find funds so residents do not pay out of pocket, suggesting part of the $1.6 billion be set aside for these households' conversions.
Proposed a program for early transitioners with grants scaled to income, larger for low earners, and said auditing could find funds for it.

Said 2050 is the year for septic conversion, and applicants for a building permit will already be asked to convert. Proposed developing a $10,000 grant or program through real property tax, noting conversion costs maybe 15 to 30,000 depending on property and terrain.

Said ʻIolani Palace had electricity before the White House and the U.S. turned Hawaiʻi into a third-world place without sewage, with profits siphoned away. Said officials waive sewage requirements for developers, and that as an independent nation Hawaiʻi would be wealthy enough to solve the problem.

Said the county would talk with the Department of Health and seek an extension if 2050 is not realistic, along with grants, loans and federal, state and EPA funding. Said some Lahaina properties got on county sewer during recovery, and noted septic systems need more land for a leach field.

Said he too must install a septic system and that vertical systems need less leach field land. Proposed real property tax adjustments and county purchasing deals with retailers to cut the cost of tanks and parts.

Said many who cannot afford conversion are kūpuna, and proposed the county do the work first and recover the cost through taxes. Proposed seeking federal money, up to $30,000 times 2,200 systems, to finish now rather than wait 24 years.

Said her own system cost $80,000 due to blue rock, so $30,000 is wishful thinking, and the EPA set the 2050 deadline 18 years ago with no extension expected. Proposed learning from countries such as Vanuatu, Tonga and Samoa and seeking federal health grants.

Said he worked three and a half years on a regional wastewater reclamation project and has a plan for each of 41 injection wells. Proposed bioreactor gardens instead of septic tanks and an irrigation reuse greenbelt firebreak, said he got a lymphatic condition after swimming, and said he cannot rule out a coordinated biological attack.
